modelo-base.d: The checkpoint that comes out of next-token pretraining: it completes text, but has no conversation format, doesn't know when to stop, doesn't follow instructions reliably and has no safety policy. It is the starting point of post-training.

modelo-instruct.d: A base model post-trained to converse in turns (chat template, end of turn), follow instructions, use tools and refuse what it should. The milestone is InstructGPT (2022), whose 1.3B model was preferred over the 175B GPT-3.

sft.d: Supervised fine-tuning: maximum likelihood of the responses in demonstrations, with cross-entropy on the assistant tokens only. It is off-policy (it minimizes the forward KL from the data to the model) and it is the first stage, and the reference, of almost every other method.

rlhf.d: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: human preferences train a reward model, and the policy is optimized against it with RL (classically PPO), tied to the SFT model by a KL penalty. InstructGPT's canonical pipeline: SFT → RM → PPO.

reward-model.d: A network that gives a response a scalar score. In classic RLHF it is the LM itself with a scalar head read at the last token, trained with Bradley–Terry on preference pairs: \(-\log\sigma(r_w - r_l)\). Only score differences matter.

rlvr.d: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (a term coined by Tülu 3): RL in which the reward model is replaced by a verification function (answer key, code tests, format regex). It rewards only when the answer is verifiably correct; it is the engine behind reasoning models.

verificador.d: An executable function (not a trained network) that checks a response: equivalence with the answer key in \boxed{}, test cases, F2P/P2P tests in a repository, a format regex. It is the reward source of RLVR; if it is lax, it can be hacked.

cold-start.d: A short SFT on a few thousand long, readable chains of thought, applied before reasoning RL (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3). It fixes problems of running RL directly on the base, such as R1-Zero's poor readability and language mixing.

rft.d: Generate several responses per prompt, keep only the approved ones (verifier, tests or RM) and do SFT on them, possibly over several rounds (STaR, ReST). It is equivalent to a policy gradient with a binary reward in which the negatives are discarded. This is how R1 generated ~600K reasoning examples.

reward-hacking.d: When the policy finds a shortcut the judge rewards that isn't the desired behavior: verbose answers that please an RM with a length bias, copying the source text, repeated tool calls just below a penalty threshold. It is Goodhart's law in practice; the KL leash is one of the defenses.

destilacao-on-policy.d: The student generates its own responses and a teacher gives, at each position, its log-probability for the token written; the per-token advantage is \(\log\pi_T(y_t) - \log\pi_\theta(y_t)\). It combines SFT's dense signal with RL's on-policy sampling and minimizes a reverse KL.

modelo-de-referencia.d: A frozen copy of the policy, almost always the SFT checkpoint, against which drift is measured: \(\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\) in RLHF, the log-ratio \(\log\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}\) in DPO. It costs memory and forward passes; with LoRA, it can be the base itself with the adapters switched off.

politica.d: In RL, the rule the agent uses to choose actions: a distribution \(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\). In an LLM, the action is the next token and the state is the prompt plus the prefix generated so far; the policy is the model being trained itself, with weights \(\theta\).

on-policy.d: Training on data generated by the very policy being trained (\(\mu = \pi_\theta\)), in the states it visits. PPO, GRPO, on-policy distillation and MOPD are on-policy; in practice only approximately, because the inference engine and the training engine don't produce identical log-probs.

off-policy.d: Training on data generated by another policy (\(\mu \neq \pi_\theta\)): humans, a teacher or an old version of the model. SFT, off-policy distillation, offline DPO and AWR are off-policy.

vies-de-exposicao.d: SFT's mismatch between training and generation: in training, each position sees the dataset's perfect prefix (teacher forcing); in generation, it sees its own prefix, mistakes included. One deviation leads to never-seen states and the errors compound. On-policy methods train precisely on those states.

kl-direto-reverso.d: \(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\) (forward) punishes the model \(q\) wherever it gives little mass to something the target \(p\) does: it is mass-covering, and it is what SFT minimizes. \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\) (reverse) punishes mass where the target puts none: it is mode-seeking, and it is what RL with KL and on-policy distillation minimize.

bradley-terry.d: A model of paired comparisons (1952): \(P(y_w \succ y_l) = \sigma(r_w - r_l)\). The reward difference is the log-odds of the preference, and only differences matter. It is the basis of the loss for reward models and for DPO.

rlaif.d: RL from AI Feedback: the preference pairs are labeled by an LLM (in Constitutional AI, guided by written principles) instead of humans; a preference model trained on those labels becomes the RL reward. Cheap and consistent, but it inherits the judge's biases.

llm-as-judge.d: Using an LLM, instructed with a rubric or a reference, to score or compare responses in place of a human; in 2025–26 it becomes an RL reward for hard-to-verify tasks (generative judges with rubrics in DeepSeek-V3.2/V4, GLM-5 and MiMo). It has position, verbosity and self-preference biases.

coeficiente-de-gradiente.d: A lens from the DeepSeekMath paper: SFT, RFT, PPO, GRPO and on-policy distillation all have the form \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{GC}_t\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(o_t)]\); only the data source and each token's weight \(\mathrm{GC}_t\) change (1 in SFT, the group advantage in GRPO, \(\log\pi_T - \log\pi_\theta\) in OPD).

ppo.d: A policy-gradient algorithm (Schulman et al., 2017) that reuses each batch for a few epochs and limits the step by cutting off the incentive when the ratio \(\rho = \pi_\theta/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\) leaves \([1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]\). In RLHF it uses a critic (GAE) and the RM reward minus the KL penalty.

dpo.d: Method by Rafailov et al. (2023) that optimizes preferences directly, with no explicit reward model and no RL, using the closed-form solution \(\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\,e^{r/\beta}\): loss \(-\log\sigma(\beta[h_\theta(y_w) - h_\theta(y_l)])\), with \(h_\theta = \log\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}\).

ipo.d: A variant of the ΨPO framework (Azar et al., 2023) with a quadratic loss, which drives the log-ratio margin to a finite target \(1/(2\tau)\) instead of pushing it to infinity; it does not overfit deterministic preferences. The name “Identity Policy Optimization” that sometimes circulates is not the paper's.

kto.d: Method by Ethayarajh et al. (2024) that learns from binary desirable/undesirable labels, without pairs, using a utility inspired by prospect theory relative to a reference point (the KL estimated over the batch). It needs \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\).

simpo.d: Method by Meng, Xia and Chen (2024) with no reference model: the reward is the mean per-token log-prob, \(\frac{\beta}{|y|}\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\), in a logistic loss with a target margin \(\gamma\). It saves memory; with no explicit KL, it calls for a conservative LR.

grpo.d: A critic-free variant of PPO (DeepSeekMath, 2024): it generates \(G\) responses per prompt and uses the group's \((r_i - \text{mean})/\text{std}\) as the advantage, the same for every token of the response; the KL (\(k_3\) estimator) goes into the loss. Popularized by DeepSeek-R1.

awr.d: Method by Peng et al. (2019): supervised regression of the policy weighted by \(e^{A/\beta}\), with the advantage coming from a critic \(V\), on data from a behavior policy. It shares with RLHF the shape of the KL-regularized optimum, \(\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\,e^{r/\beta}\).

rl-assincrono.d: Decoupling rollout generation (inference engine) from training, so that neither side waits for the other: batch \(i+1\) is generated while training on batch \(i\). The price is staleness (data from weights one or more versions behind), corrected with importance weights or discarding.
